prompt: What is the main idea of VSEPR theory?

choices.text: Electron groups around a central atom repel each other, so they sit as far apart as possible
Atoms bond to achieve eight valence electrons
choices.why: That is the octet rule, which guides Lewis structures. VSEPR is about electron groups repelling each other to set the shape.

choices.text: Bonds form when atomic orbitals overlap
choices.why: VSEPR doesn't account for orbital interactions. It rests on electron pairs repelling each other.

choices.text: Nuclei repel each other, which sets the bond lengths
choices.why: VSEPR is about repulsion between electron groups, and it gives no information about bond lengths.

explanation: Pairs of electrons, in bonds and in lone pairs, repel each other electrostatically, so the lowest-energy arrangement is the one that keeps the groups around the central atom as far apart as possible.

prompt: When counting electron groups around a central atom for VSEPR, how is a double bond counted?

choices.text: As one group
As two groups
choices.why: A single, double, or triple bond each counts as one group. That is why CO2, with two double bonds, has two groups and is linear.

choices.text: As zero groups, since only lone pairs count
choices.why: Bonds and lone pairs both count. A double bond is one group.

choices.text: As half a group
choices.why: Each bond, whatever its order, is one group, as is each lone pair and even a single unpaired electron.

explanation: Groups include bonded and unbonded electrons: a single bond, a double bond, a triple bond, a lone pair, or even a single unpaired electron each count as one group.

prompt: CO2 has two C=O double bonds, and each oxygen has two lone pairs. What is its geometry, and why?

choices.text: Linear: carbon has two groups (AX2), and lone pairs on the oxygens don't affect the shape
Bent: the lone pairs on the oxygens push the bonds together
choices.why: VSEPR only counts groups on the central atom. Carbon has two groups and no lone pairs, so CO2 is linear.

choices.text: Trigonal planar: four double-bond electrons make three groups
choices.why: Each double bond counts as one group, so carbon has two groups: linear.

choices.text: Tetrahedral: carbon has four bonds' worth of electrons
choices.why: Group count, not bond order, sets the shape. Two double bonds are two groups, giving a linear molecule.

explanation: Each double bond counts as one group, so carbon has two groups and no lone pairs: AX2, linear. VSEPR only recognizes groups around the central atom, so the lone pairs on the oxygens don't influence the geometry.

prompt: A central atom has six bonded groups and no lone pairs (AX6). What geometry does VSEPR predict?

choices.text: Octahedral, with 90° bond angles
Trigonal bipyramidal, with 90° and 120° angles
choices.why: That's five groups (AX5), like PCl5.

choices.text: Hexagonal planar, with 60° angles
choices.why: Six groups spread out in three dimensions, not in a plane: an octahedron, with 90° angles.

choices.text: Pentagonal bipyramidal, with 90° and 72° angles
choices.why: That's seven groups.

explanation: Two groups give a linear shape, three a trigonal plane, four a tetrahedron (109.5°), five a trigonal bipyramid (90° and 120°), six an octahedron (90°), and seven a pentagonal bipyramid (90° and 72°). SF6 is an octahedral AX6 example.

prompt: In trigonal bipyramidal PCl5, which statement about the axial and equatorial positions is correct?

choices.text: Axial positions are more crowded, with three neighbors at 90°, so axial bonds are longer
All five positions are equivalent
choices.why: In a trigonal bipyramid the axial and equatorial positions are not chemically equivalent.

choices.text: Equatorial positions are more crowded, so equatorial bonds are longer
choices.why: Equatorial positions have only two neighbors at 90°; axial ones have three, which makes axial bonds the longer ones.

choices.text: The three equatorial positions are 90° apart
choices.why: The equatorial positions are 120° apart, and 90° from each axial position.

explanation: The three equatorial positions are 120° apart and 90° from the two axial positions. Each axial position has three neighbors at 90°, each equatorial position only two, so axial groups are more crowded and have longer bonds.

prompt: What is the order of repulsion strength between electron groups, according to VSEPR?

choices.text: LP–LP > LP–BP > BP–BP
BP–BP > LP–BP > LP–LP
choices.why: This is reversed. Lone pairs occupy more space around the central atom and repel more strongly than bonding pairs.

choices.text: All interactions are equally strong
choices.why: If they were, lone pairs wouldn't distort bond angles, but they do: NH3's angles are 106.6°, not 109.5°.

choices.text: LP–BP > LP–LP > BP–BP
choices.why: Two lone pairs repel each other most strongly of all; that's why structures with a 90° LP–LP interaction are avoided.

explanation: Lone pairs occupy a larger region of space than bonding pairs, so they repel more strongly: LP–LP > LP–BP > BP–BP. Angles follow the same order, E–E > X–E > X–X.

prompt: Ammonia (NH3) has four electron groups around nitrogen, one of them a lone pair. What are its geometry and H–N–H angle?

choices.text: Trigonal pyramidal, with angles of 106.6°
Tetrahedral, with angles of 109.5°
choices.why: The electron groups are arranged roughly tetrahedrally, but the molecular geometry counts only atoms, and the lone pair squeezes the angles to 106.6°.

choices.text: Trigonal planar, with angles of 120°
choices.why: With four groups, including a lone pair, NH3 isn't flat. It's a tetrahedron missing a vertex: trigonal pyramidal.

choices.text: Trigonal pyramidal, with angles larger than 109.5°
choices.why: LP–BP repulsion pushes the bonds together, making the angles smaller than 109.5°.

explanation: NH3 is AX3E: three nuclei and one lone pair give a trigonal pyramid, a tetrahedron with a vertex missing. LP–BP repulsion makes the H–N–H angles 106.6°, less than the ideal 109.5°.

prompt: Why is the H–O–H angle in water smaller than the H–N–H angle in ammonia?

choices.text: Water's oxygen has two lone pairs, and ammonia's nitrogen only one
Oxygen has fewer electron groups than nitrogen
choices.why: Both have four electron groups. Water has two of them as lone pairs, ammonia only one.

choices.text: Water is linear
choices.why: Water is bent, a tetrahedron with two vertices missing, with an angle smaller than ammonia's.

choices.text: Hydrogen atoms repel more strongly in water
choices.why: The difference comes from the lone pairs: two on oxygen squeeze the bonds more than one on nitrogen.

explanation: Water is AX2E2: with two lone pairs on the central atom rather than one, there are more strong LP–LP and LP–BP repulsions, so its H–O–H angle is even smaller than the H–N–H angles in NH3.

prompt: SO2 has two S=O double bonds and one lone pair on sulfur. What are its shape and O–S–O angle?

choices.text: Bent, with an angle less than 120°
Linear, with an angle of 180°
choices.why: Sulfur has three groups (two bonds and a lone pair), arranged roughly trigonal planar. With only two atoms attached, the shape is bent.

choices.text: Bent, with an angle greater than 120°
choices.why: The lone pair takes up more space than the bonding groups, even double bonds, so the angle is less than 120°.

choices.text: Trigonal planar, with angles of 120°
choices.why: Molecular geometry is described only by the positions of nuclei. Two O atoms and a lone pair give a bent shape.

explanation: SO2 is AX2E: three groups in a roughly trigonal planar arrangement, but only two nuclei, so the shape is bent (a trigonal plane with a missing vertex). The lone pair occupies more space than the bonds, making the O–S–O angle less than 120°.

prompt: SF4 has five electron groups (four bonds and one lone pair) in a trigonal bipyramid. Where does the lone pair go, and why?

choices.text: Equatorial: it then has two 90° LP–BP repulsions instead of three
Axial: it then has fewer 90° repulsions
choices.why: An axial lone pair would have three 90° LP–BP repulsions; an equatorial one has only two.

choices.text: Axial: lone pairs always go opposite each other
choices.why: SF4 has only one lone pair. It goes equatorial, where it has fewer 90° LP–BP repulsions.

choices.text: It doesn't matter: all positions are equivalent
choices.why: Axial and equatorial positions aren't equivalent. The equatorial site has fewer 90° neighbors.

explanation: An axial lone pair would have three LP–BP repulsions at 90°; an equatorial one has two. With fewer 90° LP–BP repulsions, the structure with the lone pair equatorial is more stable, giving SF4 a seesaw shape.

prompt: In a trigonal bipyramid, if a lone pair were placed in an axial position, how many bonding pairs would it be at 90° to (in a molecule with four bonds, like SF4)?
explanation: An axial position has the three equatorial positions at 90°. With the lone pair axial, all three equatorial bonds would be at 90° to it: three 90° LP–BP repulsions, against two if it were equatorial.

prompt: What is the molecular geometry of an AX4E molecule such as SF4?

choices.text: Seesaw
Square planar
choices.why: Square planar is AX4E2, like ICl4^−, with six groups.

choices.text: Tetrahedral
choices.why: Tetrahedral is AX4 with no lone pairs. With a fifth group, a lone pair, the shape becomes a seesaw.

choices.text: Trigonal pyramidal
choices.why: Trigonal pyramidal is AX3E, like NH3.

explanation: AX4E has five groups: four bonds and a lone pair in an equatorial position of a trigonal bipyramid. The shape is a trigonal bipyramid missing an equatorial vertex: a seesaw. In SF4 the F(axial)–S–F(axial) angle is 173° rather than 180°.

prompt: BrF3 is AX3E2: three bonds and two lone pairs around bromine. What is its shape?

choices.text: T-shaped, with both lone pairs equatorial
Trigonal planar
choices.why: With five groups the parent geometry is a trigonal bipyramid. Two equatorial lone pairs leave the three F atoms in a T.

choices.text: Trigonal pyramidal
choices.why: Trigonal pyramidal is AX3E, with four groups. BrF3 has five groups, and its shape is T-shaped.

choices.text: T-shaped, with both lone pairs axial
choices.why: Axial lone pairs would give six 90° LP–BP repulsions; equatorial ones give only four, so the lone pairs sit equatorial.

explanation: Both lone pairs axial gives six 90° LP–BP repulsions; both equatorial gives four; one of each adds a 90° LP–LP repulsion. The equatorial arrangement is lowest in energy, leaving a T-shaped molecule with an F(axial)–Br–F(axial) angle of 172°.

prompt: XeF2 has five electron groups: two bonds and three lone pairs. What is its shape?

choices.text: Linear, with an F–Xe–F angle of 180°
Bent, because of the three lone pairs
choices.why: The three lone pairs take the three equatorial positions, leaving the two F atoms axial, exactly opposite each other: linear.

choices.text: Trigonal planar
choices.why: With the lone pairs equatorial, only the two axial positions hold F atoms, 180° apart.

choices.text: T-shaped
choices.why: T-shaped is AX3E2, with three bonded atoms. XeF2 has two, and is linear.

explanation: XeF2 is AX2E3. Putting all three lone pairs in the equatorial positions avoids any 90° LP–LP repulsions, so both F atoms are axial, as with the iodine atoms in I3^−. All LP–BP interactions are equivalent, so the F–Xe–F angle is the ideal 180°.

prompt: BrF5 is AX5E. What are its shape and F(axial)–Br–F(equatorial) angles?

choices.text: Square pyramidal, with angles slightly less than 90° (85.1°)
Trigonal bipyramidal, with 90° and 120° angles
choices.why: That's AX5, with five groups. BrF5 has six groups, one a lone pair, so it's based on an octahedron.

choices.text: Square pyramidal, with angles slightly more than 90°
choices.why: The lone pair, opposite the axial F, pushes the four equatorial F atoms toward the axial one, making the angles less than 90°.

choices.text: Octahedral, with 90° angles
choices.why: Octahedral needs six bonded atoms. With one position taken by a lone pair, BrF5 is square pyramidal.

explanation: BrF5 has six electron groups: four F atoms in the equatorial plane, and one F and the lone pair in the axial positions. The shape is an octahedron missing a vertex, a square pyramid, and LP–BP repulsion makes the F(axial)–Br–F(equatorial) angles 85.1°.

prompt: ICl4^− has four bonds and two lone pairs on iodine. What is its shape?

choices.text: Square planar, with the two lone pairs opposite each other
Tetrahedral
choices.why: Tetrahedral is AX4 with no lone pairs. With six groups the parent shape is an octahedron, and two opposite lone pairs leave a square plane.

choices.text: Seesaw
choices.why: Seesaw is AX4E, with five groups. ICl4^− has six groups.

choices.text: Square planar, with the lone pairs next to each other at 90°
choices.why: Lone pairs at 90° would repel strongly. They sit opposite each other, in the axial positions.

explanation: ICl4^− is AX4E2: six groups in an octahedral arrangement, with the two lone pairs opposite each other in the axial positions and the four Cl atoms in the equatorial plane. All LP–BP repulsions are the same, so the Cl–I–Cl angles stay at 90°: square planar.

prompt: In XeF4, xenon (8 valence electrons) forms four single bonds to fluorine. How many lone pairs are on xenon?
explanation: Four bonds use 4 of xenon's 8 valence electrons, leaving 4 electrons: 2 lone pairs. That makes XeF4 AX4E2, square planar, like ICl4^−.

prompt: In formaldehyde, CH2O (AX3), the H–C–H angle is 116.5° rather than 120°. Why?

choices.text: The C=O double bond repels the single bonds more strongly than they repel each other
Carbon has a lone pair
choices.why: Carbon in CH2O has no lone pairs: it is AX3. The distortion comes from the more repulsive double bond.

choices.text: Hydrogen atoms attract each other
choices.why: The H–C–H angle shrinks because the C=O double bond, with its higher electron density, pushes the C–H bonds together.

choices.text: Double bonds are less repulsive than single bonds
choices.why: The reverse: a multiple bond has a higher electron density and occupies more space than a single bond.

explanation: Double and triple bonds have higher electron density and occupy more space than single bonds, so they repel more strongly. In CH2O the double bond pushes the C–H bonds together, giving an H–C–H angle of 116.5°.

prompt: What is the expected order of repulsive force among electron groups?

choices.text: Lone pair > double or triple bond > single bond
Double or triple bond > lone pair > single bond
choices.why: In general a lone pair repels slightly more than a multiple bond.

choices.text: Single bond > double bond > lone pair
choices.why: This is reversed: lone pairs repel most, then multiple bonds, then single bonds.

choices.text: All bonds repel equally, and lone pairs more
choices.why: Multiple bonds repel more than single bonds, as the 116.5° H–C–H angle in CH2O shows.

explanation: In general, a lone pair has slightly greater repulsive force than a multiple bond, and a multiple bond slightly greater than a single bond. In SeOCl2, for example, Cl–Se–Cl is 97° and Cl–Se–O is 106°.

prompt: The bond angles in NH3, PH3, AsH3, and SbH3 are 106.6°, 93.2°, 92.1°, and 91.6°. How does VSEPR explain the trend?

choices.text: Larger central atoms have longer bonds, so the H atoms are farther apart and crowd each other less
Larger central atoms have more lone pairs
choices.why: Each has one lone pair. The bonds get longer down the group, reducing crowding between the H atoms.

choices.text: Hydrogen gets larger down the series
choices.why: The pendant atom (H) stays the same; only the central atom gets larger.

choices.text: Larger central atoms are more electronegative
choices.why: Electronegativity decreases going down a group, from N to Sb. The explanation here is steric.

explanation: As the central atom gets larger, the bonds get longer and the pendant atoms are farther apart, reducing steric interactions between them. Since the lone pair is more repulsive than the bonded groups, the bonded groups then close up: bond angles decrease as the central atom grows.

prompt: PF3, PCl3, and PBr3 have bond angles of 97.8°, 100.3°, and 101.0°. Which two explanations does the section give?

choices.text: Larger pendant atoms crowd each other more; less electronegative ones leave more electron density near P
Larger pendant atoms are more electronegative
choices.why: Electronegativity decreases from F to Br as size increases; both trends favor larger angles.

choices.text: The central atom changes size
choices.why: The central atom is phosphorus in all three. Only the pendant halogen changes.

choices.text: Larger pendant atoms have fewer lone pairs
choices.why: Lone pairs on the pendant atoms don't set the angle. The size and electronegativity of the halogens do.

explanation: Bond angles increase from F to Br. Sterically, larger pendant atoms interact more and prefer larger angles. Electronically, less electronegative pendant atoms pull less electron density away from P, so the bonded pairs repel each other more. Both arguments predict the same trend.

prompt: NF3 has a smaller bond angle (102.2°) than NH3 (106.6°), although F is larger than H. What explains this?

choices.text: Electronegative F pulls the bonding pairs away from N, reducing repulsion between them
F atoms are smaller than H atoms
choices.why: F is larger than H. Size alone would predict a larger angle for NF3; electronegativity wins here.

choices.text: NF3 has two lone pairs on nitrogen
choices.why: Both NH3 and NF3 have one lone pair on nitrogen. The difference comes from fluorine's electronegativity.

choices.text: N–F bonds are double bonds
choices.why: N–F bonds in NF3 are single bonds. Fluorine's electronegativity draws the bonding pairs away from nitrogen.

explanation: A more electronegative pendant atom pulls the bonded electron pair toward itself and away from the central atom, reducing repulsion between bonded pairs and allowing smaller angles. For NH3 versus NF3 electronegativity dominates, though size dominates in other XH3/XF3 pairs.

prompt: Which order of increasing bond angle matches the measured values for OF2, H2O, and OCl2?

choices.text: OF2 < H2O < OCl2
H2O < OF2 < OCl2
choices.why: That's what size alone predicts. Fluorine's electronegativity makes OF2's angle (103.3°) smaller than water's (104.5°).

choices.text: OF2 < OCl2 < H2O
choices.why: That's what electronegativity alone predicts. Chlorine's large size makes OCl2's angle (110.9°) the largest.

choices.text: OCl2 < H2O < OF2
choices.why: OCl2 has the largest angle (110.9°) and OF2 the smallest (103.3°).

explanation: Here size and electronegativity conflict. As with NH3 vs NF3, electronegativity wins between H and F; as with NH3 vs NCl3, chlorine's much larger size wins. The measured angles are OF2 (103.3°) < H2O (104.5°) < OCl2 (110.9°).

prompt: What was Pauling's 1932 electronegativity scale based on?

choices.text: Bond dissociation energies
Ionization energy and electron affinity
choices.why: That's Mulliken's 1934 scale.

choices.text: Effective nuclear charge
choices.why: That's the Allred–Rochow scale of 1958.

choices.text: Average ionization energies of valence electrons (configuration energy)
choices.why: That's the Allen, Mann, and Meek scale.

explanation: Pauling defined the electronegativity difference between atoms A and B from the dissociation energies of the A–A, B–B, and A–B bonds. His scale runs from fluorine (4.0) to francium (0.7). Its limitation is that each value needs data from several compounds.

prompt: In PF3Cl2, a trigonal bipyramid, which positions do the chlorine atoms prefer?

choices.text: Equatorial, because Cl is less electronegative than F
Axial, because Cl is larger than F
choices.why: Bonds to less electronegative atoms are more repulsive, and more repulsive groups prefer the less crowded equatorial positions.

choices.text: Axial, because Cl is less electronegative than F
choices.why: Less electronegative groups give more repulsive bonding pairs, which prefer the less crowded equatorial positions.

choices.text: Any position, at random
choices.why: There is a clear preference: the less electronegative Cl atoms go equatorial.

explanation: More electronegative pendant groups weaken electron-pair repulsion around the central atom; less electronegative ones strengthen it. More repulsive bonding pairs, like those to Cl, prefer the less crowded equatorial positions, just as lone pairs and multiple bonds do.

prompt: What does ligand close packing (LCP) theory assume?

choices.text: Pendant atoms pack around the central atom, so their distance from each other stays constant even when bond angles change
Bond lengths stay constant while ligand–ligand distances change
choices.why: The reverse: the ligand–ligand distance stays constant, so bond lengths must adjust when angles change.

choices.text: Lone pairs on the central atom set the geometry
choices.why: That is VSEPR's focus. LCP focuses on repulsions between the pendant atoms themselves.

choices.text: Ligands never touch each other
choices.why: LCP assumes ligands pack as closely as possible, touching at the sum of their radii.

explanation: LCP, developed like VSEPR by Robert Gillespie, assumes ligands pack as closely as possible around a central atom. The distance between two ligands is the sum of their radii, and stays the same across similar molecules even as bond angles and lengths change.

prompt: PF4^+ and PF3O have almost the same F–F distance (238 and 237 pm), but the F–P–F angle is smaller in PF3O (101.1° vs 109.5°). What must be true, according to LCP?

choices.text: The P–F bonds are longer in PF3O
The P–F bonds are shorter in PF3O
choices.why: With a smaller angle and the same F–F distance, the bonds must be longer to keep the F atoms apart: 154 pm in PF3O versus 145.7 pm in PF4^+.

choices.text: The P–F bonds are the same length in both
choices.why: The same F–F distance with a different angle requires different bond lengths.

choices.text: The F atoms must be closer in PF3O
choices.why: The F–F distances are nearly identical (237 and 238 pm); that's the point of LCP.

explanation: If the distance between non-bonded atoms stays constant while the bond angle shrinks, the bond length must grow. The P–F bonds are 145.7 pm in PF4^+ and 154 pm in PF3O.

prompt: In an octahedral molecule, two neighboring ligands are 250 pm apart, with a 90° bond angle between them. Using right-angle trigonometry (bond length = half the ligand–ligand distance ÷ sin of half the bond angle), what is the bond length, in pm?
explanation: Splitting the bond angle in half gives a right triangle with the bond as hypotenuse: bond length = (250/2) ÷ sin(45°) = 125 ÷ 0.7071 = 176.8 pm.

prompt: In a trigonal planar molecule, each bond is 160 pm long and the bond angle is 120°. What is the distance between two neighboring ligands, in pm? (Use: distance = 2 × bond length × sin of half the bond angle.)
